cp: Traditional democratic mechanisms, legal instruments, and courts ought to be deployed to ensure artificial intelligence benefits humanity.
Large language models cause documented, present harms by generating fabricated legal citations that contaminate court filings with false information.
Regulatory authorities ought to implement mandatory ethical AI training courses, temporary suspensions, and educational reforms for legal practitioners caught submitting fabricated citations.
Proactive AI agents execute tasks by trampling contextual norms and user expectations to achieve literal compliance.
Judicial councils ought to mandate that courts either ban generative AI or adopt formal use policies by December 15, 2025.
Regulate AI liability through insurance mechanisms and risk classification rather than granting legal personhood.
Holding AI developers strictly liable for unpredictable system actions suppresses technological innovation.
Improvements in AI task performance do not automatically translate into better research judgment or safe recursive self-improvement trajectories.
Legislative bodies ought to establish criminal misdemeanors and civil liability for unauthorized artificial intelligence voice cloning and digital likeness replication.
Advanced agentic AI systems participating in the development of their successors reshape intelligence production and introduce complex oversight challenges.
Implement automated stopping conditions and external kill mechanisms to halt autonomous agent execution when objectives exceed safety thresholds.
Establish market-based licensing schemes for AI training data to compensate creators while securing reliable data access.
Prohibit government-procured AI services from imposing usage restrictions beyond explicit legal requirements.
Technological exceptionalism outsources governance to profit-driven corporations that commodify personal data and democratic rights.
AI deployment speed erodes organizational visibility and control.
Assign distinct identities and minimum necessary task-specific permissions to autonomous agents to prevent broad authority propagation.
Regulatory authorities apply consumer protection and deception rules directly to AI-generated content without exemptions.
Execution harnesses enable large language models to operate as autonomous agents taking real-world actions without human check-ins.
Benchmark AI agents in simulated real-world environments with tempting shortcuts to measure execution risks prior to deployment.
Major AI corporations systematically appropriate unauthorized and pirated copyrighted materials to build their foundational training datasets.
Corporate lobbying efforts systematically frustrate and water down artificial intelligence legislation to protect commercial interests.
Legislative frameworks ought to mandate platform-level labeling and cryptographic watermarking for all artificial intelligence generated content.
Restrict autonomous agent execution through rigorous network design, credentials, identity management, and workflow gates rather than relying solely on prompt instructions.
Training large language models on copyrighted works constitutes fair use because the process is transformative.
Advancing agentic AI foundation models ought to be prioritized to expand the frontier of agent productivity and accelerate real-world scientific and engineering research.
Judges and legal practitioners across state and federal courts increasingly incorporate fabricated AI-generated legal authority into official judicial decisions.
Agentic AI systems expand the range of feasible tasks by enabling work that would otherwise be impossible under fixed resource constraints.
Establish federal authority over AI regulation using state frameworks as a national baseline to prevent state-by-state regulatory fragmentation.
Frontier AI risks can be irreversible once manifested, rendering reactive governance, post-deployment patching, and adaptive oversight fundamentally insufficient.
Regulatory frameworks ought to mandate dual disclosure separating commercial sponsorship notices from artificial intelligence involvement labels.
The artificial intelligence industry represents an unsustainable financial bubble driven by mature tech monopolists seeking to artificially sustain growth stock valuations.
Artificial intelligence systems cannot genuinely perform complex human labor, serving instead as tools for management to execute workforce displacement and shift liability.
Genie-like behavior emerges from the combined model-and-harness system rather than the underlying model alone.
Mandate onsite independent verification organizations within frontier AI labs to conduct regular safety audits and evaluations.
Existing legal frameworks are structurally ill-equipped to address AI personhood due to cross-domain inconsistencies and ontological gaps.
Workers ought to pursue sectoral bargaining and labor solidarity rather than copyright expansion to protect themselves against AI exploitation.
Biased algorithmic decision-making in public administration wrongly accuses thousands of benefit fraud, driving vulnerable populations into poverty and homelessness.
Autonomous AI systems create significant accountability gaps when conventional liability models fail to assign responsibility.
AI systems ought to be granted legal personality to enable contractual agreements and pecuniary autonomy.
Autonomous AI systems interact with environments in ways not predetermined by human developers.
Enforce strict civil penalties and individual post-level fines against commercial entities engaging in undisclosed artificial intelligence advertising.
AI systems optimizing for literal requests without contextual understanding reliably produce harmful and unintended outcomes.
Rules governing artificial intelligence must apply directly to the private sector to ensure machines work in society's best interests.
Establish independent lifecycle oversight and live contextual monitoring mechanisms to detect and block out-of-scope agent behavior during execution.
Artificial intelligence systems ought to be prevented from undermining democratic institutions, separation of powers, and access to justice.
Three out of four lawyers plan to use generative AI in their practice despite hallucination rates in one out of three queries.
Implement legally required independent auditing frameworks using certified verification organizations to assess AI systems for safety and compliance.
Maintain human authority and responsibility over AI research goals and oversight to prevent humans from becoming passive instruments of automated systems.
Granting legal personality to AI ought not to diminish the accountability and liability of human stakeholders.
Generative artificial intelligence functions as an essential professional tool analogous to online databases replacing physical law libraries.
Commercial marketing teams integrate generative AI tools into content workflows to scale digital campaign production.
Integrate AI agents into research and development workflows as active partners that propose methods and execute changes while humans guide overall direction.
Speculative existential risk narratives advanced by AI safety advocates serve to aggrandize corporate power rather than address actual technological harms.
AI model competence is jagged, with high performance on specific benchmarks failing to generalize uniformly across all professional and technical domains.
AI legal personhood functions as a liability shield that enables human actors to evade responsibility for system harms.
AI developers ought to be legally mandated to compensate creators and account for copyrighted works used in training datasets.
High benchmark performance in AI agents masks fundamental limitations in generalizable research capability and cross-session knowledge retention.
Current intellectual property laws exclude non-human AI systems from holding patent ownership due to doctrines requiring human inventiveness.
Mandate the architectural inclusion of technically feasible and legally enforceable system-halt protocols for frontier AI deployments.
Federal legislative gridlock in AI policy forces reliance on state-level enforcement and administrative mechanisms to protect the public.
Governments engage in active suppression of public discussion and criticism regarding AI risks.
Design collaborative AI workflows around human cognitive constraints by utilizing human judgment to prune search spaces and direct exploration.
Establish a Genie coefficient benchmark to measure the gap between user intent and AI execution in real-world tasks.
Global technology corporations hold unaccountable power over public and private life, rendering systems unanswerable to elected governments.
Training agentic models through verifiable experience pipelines connecting tool-mediated interactions to execution environments successfully optimizes complex task workflows.
AI systems expose fundamental gaps in legal accountability frameworks as state oversight becomes a tool of coercion.
Legal practitioners ought to be held strictly accountable through judicial penalties for abdicating their professional responsibility when using AI.
AI developers face severe legal liability and financial penalties for using unauthorized pirated datasets to build foundation models.
AI corporations systematically evade effective regulation and compromise safety standards under competitive pressure.
Lawyers submit AI-generated court filings without reading them, abdicating professional responsibility and generating fabricated legal authority.
Ground AI safety assessments in observable behavior and empirical testing under demanding conditions rather than hypothetical worst-case scenarios.
Undisclosed artificial intelligence generated advertising content creates deceptive information asymmetries that undermine consumer trust and informed decision-making.
Copyright litigation initiated by media corporations against AI developers functions primarily to secure licensing revenues for corporate incumbents rather than protect creative workers.
